questions.questionTextEn:
The structure of $\mathbf{Q}$ in the following reaction scheme is:
$\mathbf{M}$ (enantiopure D-arabinose, Fischer projection top-to-bottom: $\text{CHO}$, $\text{C2}: \text{HO—C—H}$, $\text{C3}: \text{H—C—OH}$, $\text{C4}: \text{H—C—OH}$, $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$) $\xrightarrow{\text{PhNHNH}_2\text{ (excess)}} \mathbf{N}$; $\mathbf{P} \xrightarrow{\text{PhNHNH}_2\text{ (excess)}} \mathbf{N}$; $\mathbf{P} \xrightarrow{\text{H}_2,\; \text{Ni}} \mathbf{Q}$.
questions.explanationEn:
Step 1: $\mathbf{M}$ is D-arabinose. Treatment of an aldose with excess phenylhydrazine ($\text{PhNHNH}_2$) destroys the stereocenter at $\text{C2}$ to form an osazone ($\mathbf{N}$).
Step 2: Since aldose $\mathbf{P}$ gives the same osazone $\mathbf{N}$ as $\mathbf{M}$, $\mathbf{P}$ must be the $\text{C2}$-epimer of D-arabinose, which is D-ribose (Fischer projection: $\text{CHO}$, $\text{C2}: \text{H—C—OH}$, $\text{C3}: \text{H—C—OH}$, $\text{C4}: \text{H—C—OH}$, $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$).
Step 3: Catalytic hydrogenation of D-ribose ($\mathbf{P}$) with $\text{H}_2/\text{Ni}$ reduces the aldehyde ($\text{CHO}$) group to $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ without altering the $\text{C2}$–$\text{C4}$ stereocenters, yielding ribitol (all three $\text{OH}$ groups on the right in the Fischer projection), which is option (B).

questions.questionTextEn:
The major product of the reaction is:
5,5-dimethylcyclohex-2-en-1-one $\xrightarrow{\text{(i) } \text{CH}_2\text{I}_2,\; \text{Zn–Cu};\; \text{(ii) } \text{Li},\; \text{NH}_3\text{ (liq.)};\; \text{(iii) } \text{H}_3\text{O}^+}$
questions.explanationEn:
Step 1: Treatment of 5,5-dimethylcyclohex-2-en-1-one with $\text{CH}_2\text{I}_2$ and $\text{Zn–Cu}$ (Simmons–Smith reaction) cyclopropanates the $\text{C2}=\text{C3}$ double bond to form 4,4-dimethylbicyclo[4.1.0]heptan-2-one.
Step 2: Dissolving-metal reduction with $\text{Li/NH}_3\text{ (liq.)}$ transfers electrons into the carbonyl $\pi^*$ orbital, triggering regioselective reductive cleavage of the cyclopropane bond that best overlaps with the carbonyl $\pi$ system (the exo $\text{C1–C7}$ bond adjacent to the carbonyl). This leaves the $\text{CH}_2$ carbon attached to the $\beta$-carbon ($\text{C3}$) as a methyl group.
Step 3: Acidic workup ($\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$) protonates the resulting enolate to afford 3,3,5-trimethylcyclohexan-1-one, which is option (A).

questions.questionTextEn:
The rate of addition of 1-hexyl radical to the given molecules follows the order:
$\mathbf{P}$: methyl acrylate ($\text{H}_2\text{C}=\text{CH–CO}_2\text{Me}$); $\mathbf{Q}$: methyl $(E)$-but-2-enoate ($\text{Me–CH}=\text{CH–CO}_2\text{Me}$); $\mathbf{R}$: dimethyl methylenemalonate ($\text{H}_2\text{C}=\text{C(CO}_2\text{Me)}_2$).
questions.explanationEn:
Step 1: The 1-hexyl radical is a nucleophilic (electron-rich) alkyl radical with a high-energy SOMO, so it reacts fastest with electron-deficient alkenes having a low-energy LUMO and minimal steric hindrance at the site of attack.
Step 2: Compound $\mathbf{R}$ ($\text{H}_2\text{C}=\text{C(CO}_2\text{Me)}_2$) has two strongly electron-withdrawing $-\text{CO}_2\text{Me}$ groups stabilizing the resulting radical and lowering the alkene LUMO, while its terminal $=\text{CH}_2$ carbon is sterically unhindered; hence $\mathbf{R}$ reacts fastest.
Step 3: Compound $\mathbf{P}$ ($\text{H}_2\text{C}=\text{CH–CO}_2\text{Me}$) has one $-\text{CO}_2\text{Me}$ group and an unhindered terminal $=\text{CH}_2$, whereas $\mathbf{Q}$ ($\text{Me–CH}=\text{CH–CO}_2\text{Me}$) has an electron-donating and sterically hindering $\beta$-methyl group that slows radical addition.
Therefore, the rate order is $\mathbf{R} > \mathbf{P} > \mathbf{Q}$, which is option (C).

questions.questionTextEn:
The major product of the reaction is:
1,1,2-tribromocyclohexane isotopologue [at $\text{C1}$: $\text{Br}^*$ (up/wedge) and $\text{H}$ (down/dash); at $\text{C2}$: $\text{Br}$ (up/wedge) and $\text{Br}^*$ (down/dash), where $\text{Br}^* = {}^{82}\text{Br}$] $\xrightarrow{\text{NaI},\; \text{MeOH},\; 110\;^\circ\text{C}}$
questions.explanationEn:
Step 1: Iodide ion ($\text{I}^-$ from $\text{NaI}$) induces a stereospecific anti-periplanar E2 debromination of vicinal dibromides.
Step 2: In the given cyclohexane derivative, the substituents at $\text{C1}$ are $\text{Br}^*$ (up) and $\text{H}$ (down), while at $\text{C2}$ they are $\text{Br}$ (up) and $\text{Br}^*$ (down). Thus, the two bromine atoms that are *trans* (capable of adopting a *trans*-diaxial anti-periplanar arrangement) are the $\text{Br}^*$ on $\text{C1}$ (up) and the $\text{Br}^*$ on $\text{C2}$ (down).
Step 3: Anti-elimination removes both labeled $\text{Br}^*$ atoms (forming $\text{IBr}^*$ and $(\text{Br}^*)^-$), leaving the unlabeled $\text{Br}$ atom attached to the double bond to yield 1-bromocyclohex-1-ene, which is option (A).

questions.questionTextEn: The diagram that best describes the variation of viscosity ($\eta$) of water with temperature at $1\text{ atm}$ is:
optionsEn: Plot of $\eta / \text{cP}$ vs. Temperature ($0$ to $100\;^\circ\text{C}$) showing a smooth, concave-up exponential-like decrease from $\approx 1.8\text{ cP}$ at $0\;^\circ\text{C}$ to $\approx 0.28\text{ cP}$ at $100\;^\circ\text{C}$
Plot of $\eta / \text{cP}$ vs. Temperature ($0$ to $100\;^\circ\text{C}$) showing a horizontal straight line (constant $\eta \approx 1.5\text{ cP}$)
Plot of $\eta / \text{cP}$ vs. Temperature ($0$ to $100\;^\circ\text{C}$) showing a concave-down increase with temperature
Plot of $\eta / \text{cP}$ vs. Temperature ($0$ to $100\;^\circ\text{C}$) showing a linear decrease with temperature
questions.explanationEn:
Step 1: The viscosity of a liquid such as water decreases non-linearly with increasing temperature because thermal energy disrupts intermolecular hydrogen bonding and lowers the activation barrier for flow.
Step 2: Mathematically, liquid viscosity follows an Arrhenius-type (Andrade) relation, $\eta(T) = A\exp\left(\frac{E_a}{RT}\right)$, which produces a steep, concave-up curve decreasing monotonically from $1.79\text{ cP}$ at $0\;^\circ\text{C}$ to $0.89\text{ cP}$ at $25\;^\circ\text{C}$ and $0.28\text{ cP}$ at $100\;^\circ\text{C}$.
Therefore, the concave-up decreasing curve in option (A) best describes the viscosity of water.

questions.questionTextEn: The SI unit of the molar conductivity of an electrolyte solution is
questions.explanationEn:
Molar conductivity is defined as $\Lambda_m = \frac{\kappa}{c}$, where $\kappa$ is the electrical conductivity (SI unit: $\text{S m}^{-1}$) and $c$ is the molar concentration (SI unit: $\text{mol m}^{-3}$).
Therefore, the SI unit of $\Lambda_m$ is:
$\frac{\text{S m}^{-1}}{\text{mol m}^{-3}} = \text{S m}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}$.
Hence, option (D) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: The system with the lowest zero-point energy when it is confined to a one-dimensional box of length $L$ is
questions.explanationEn:
For a particle of mass $m$ confined to a 1D box of length $L$, the energy levels are $E_n = \frac{n^2 h^2}{8mL^2}$.
The zero-point energy ($n = 1$) is $E_1 = \frac{h^2}{8mL^2}$, which is inversely proportional to the mass $m$ ($E_1 \propto \frac{1}{m}$).
Among an electron ($m_e$), a proton ($\approx 1\text{ u}$), a hydrogen atom ($\approx 1\text{ u}$), and a helium atom ($\approx 4\text{ u}$), the helium atom has the largest mass and therefore the lowest zero-point energy.
Hence, option (C) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: The metal ion present in human *carbonic anhydrase* is
questions.explanationEn:
Human carbonic anhydrase is a zinc-containing metalloenzyme that catalyzes the reversible hydration of $\text{CO}_2$ to $\text{HCO}_3^-$ and $\text{H}^+$.
Its active site contains a tetrahedrally coordinated $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ ion bound to three histidine nitrogen atoms and one water/hydroxide molecule.
Hence, option (C) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: The oxoacid of sulfur that has $\text{S–O–S}$ bond is
questions.explanationEn:
Comparing the structures of the four sulfur oxoacids:
- Pyrosulfuric acid ($\text{H}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_7$, oleum): $\text{HO–SO}_2\text{–O–SO}_2\text{–OH}$, which contains a bridging $\text{S–O–S}$ linkage.
- Pyrosulfurous acid ($\text{H}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_5$): $\text{HO–SO}_2\text{–SO–OH}$, which has an unsymmetrical $\text{S–S}$ bond.
- Dithionous acid ($\text{H}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_4$): $\text{HO–SO–SO–OH}$, which has an $\text{S–S}$ bond.
- Dithionic acid ($\text{H}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_6$): $\text{HO–SO}_2\text{–SO}_2\text{–OH}$, which has an $\text{S–S}$ bond.
Hence, option (A) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: An alkaline ($\text{NaOH}$) solution of a compound produces a yellow colored solution on addition of $\text{NaBO}_3$. The compound is
questions.explanationEn:
In alkaline ($\text{NaOH}$) solution, amphoteric $\text{Cr(OH)}_3$ dissolves to form green chromite ions, $[\text{Cr(OH)}_4]^-$.
Sodium perborate ($\text{NaBO}_3$) acts as a source of $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ in aqueous alkaline medium and oxidizes $\text{Cr(III)}$ to yellow chromate ion ($\text{CrO}_4^{2-}$):
$2\text{Cr(OH)}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}_2 + 4\text{OH}^- \rightarrow 2\text{CrO}_4^{2-} \text{ (yellow)} + 8\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
Hence, option (C) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn:
The major product of the reaction is:
Pivalaldehyde ($\text{(CH}_3)_3\text{C–CHO}$) $\xrightarrow{\text{(i) } \text{BrCH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{Et},\; \text{Zn};\; \text{(ii) } \text{TsOH},\; \text{heat};\; \text{(iii) } \text{NiCl}_2,\; \text{NaBH}_4}$
questions.explanationEn:
Step 1: Reformatsky reaction of pivalaldehyde ($t\text{-BuCHO}$) with $\text{BrCH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{Et}$ and $\text{Zn}$ produces the $\beta$-hydroxy ester $t\text{-Bu–CH(OH)–CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{Et}$.
Step 2: Acid-catalyzed dehydration with $\text{TsOH}$ and heat forms the $\alpha,\beta$-unsaturated ester $(E)\text{-}t\text{-Bu–CH}=\text{CH–CO}_2\text{Et}$.
Step 3: $\text{NiCl}_2/\text{NaBH}_4$ generates nickel boride in situ, which chemoselectively reduces the conjugated $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond while leaving the ester ($-\text{CO}_2\text{Et}$) intact, giving ethyl 4,4-dimethylpentanoate ($t\text{-Bu–CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{Et}$).
Hence, option (D) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn:
The major product in the following reaction is:
4a-(dimethylsulfoniomethyl)-4,4a,5,6,7,8-hexahydronaphthalen-2(3$H$)-one (a $\Delta^{1(8\text{a})}$-2-octalone bearing an angular $-\text{CH}_2\text{S}^+\text{Me}_2$ group at $\text{C4a}$) $\xrightarrow{\text{(i) } \text{NaH};\; \text{(ii) } \text{Raney-Ni/H}_2}$
optionsEn: 4a-methyl-octahydronaphthalen-2(1$H$)-one with a cyclopropane ring fused at $\text{C8–C8a}$
1-methyl-octahydronaphthalen-2(1$H$)-one with a cyclopropane ring fused across $\text{C4a–C8a}$
4a-methyl-octahydronaphthalen-2(1$H$)-one with a cyclopropane ring fused across the former enone $\text{C1–C8a}$ bond
4a-methyl-octahydronaphthalene with a spiro-epoxide at $\text{C2}$ (replacing the carbonyl oxygen)
questions.explanationEn:
Step 1: $\text{NaH}$ deprotonates one of the less-hindered methyl groups on the sulfonium moiety ($-\text{CH}_2\text{S}^+\text{Me}_2$) to generate the sulfonium ylide $-\text{CH}_2\text{S}^+(\text{Me})\text{CH}_2^-$.
Step 2: Intramolecular Corey–Chaykovsky conjugate addition of this ylide onto the $\text{C1}=\text{C8a}$ enone double bond, followed by ring closure and displacement of the tethered thioether ($-\text{CH}_2\text{SMe}$), installs a cyclopropane ring across $\text{C1–C8a}$ while leaving $-\text{CH}_2\text{SMe}$ attached to $\text{C4a}$.
Step 3: Treatment with $\text{Raney-Ni/H}_2$ performs reductive desulfurization of the $\text{C4a–CH}_2\text{SMe}$ group to an angular methyl group ($\text{C4a–CH}_3$), leaving the $\text{C1–C8a}$ cyclopropane ring and $\text{C2}$ carbonyl intact.
Hence, option (C) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn:
The most stable conformation of $\mathbf{Y}$ and that of $\mathbf{Z}$ are:
$\mathbf{Y}$: *cis*-1,3-di-*tert*-butylcyclohexane (both $^t\text{Bu}$ groups dashed); $\mathbf{Z}$: *trans*-1,3-di-*tert*-butylcyclohexane (one $^t\text{Bu}$ wedged, one $^t\text{Bu}$ dashed).
optionsEn: $\mathbf{Y}$: chair with both $^t\text{Bu}$ equatorial; $\mathbf{Z}$: chair with one $^t\text{Bu}$ axial and one $^t\text{Bu}$ equatorial
$\mathbf{Y}$: chair with both $^t\text{Bu}$ equatorial; $\mathbf{Z}$: twist-boat with both $^t\text{Bu}$ pseudo-equatorial
$\mathbf{Y}$: twist-boat with both $^t\text{Bu}$ pseudo-equatorial; $\mathbf{Z}$: chair with one $^t\text{Bu}$ axial and one $^t\text{Bu}$ equatorial
$\mathbf{Y}$: twist-boat with both $^t\text{Bu}$ pseudo-equatorial; $\mathbf{Z}$: twist-boat with both $^t\text{Bu}$ pseudo-equatorial
questions.explanationEn:
Step 1: In *cis*-1,3-di-*tert*-butylcyclohexane ($\mathbf{Y}$), the standard chair conformation places both bulky $^t\text{Bu}$ groups in equatorial positions (1,3-diequatorial), completely avoiding 1,3-diaxial repulsion. Thus, the chair is overwhelmingly the most stable conformation for $\mathbf{Y}$.
Step 2: In *trans*-1,3-di-*tert*-butylcyclohexane ($\mathbf{Z}$), any chair conformation forces one $^t\text{Bu}$ group to be axial, incurring a severe steric penalty ($A$-value $\approx 20.5\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$). Converting to a twist-boat conformation costs about $23\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ for cyclohexane itself, but relieves the axial $^t\text{Bu}$ clash by placing both $^t\text{Bu}$ groups in pseudo-equatorial positions, making the twist-boat more stable than the chair.
Hence, option (B) is correct.

optionsEn: *dl*-1,2-dibromo-1,2-diphenylethane (zigzag representation with anti $\text{Ph}$ groups, one $\text{Br}$ dashed and one $\text{Br}$ wedged)
*meso*-1,2-dibromo-1,2-diphenylethane (zigzag representation with anti $\text{Ph}$ groups, both $\text{Br}$ groups wedged)
questions.explanationEn:
Step 1: Reaction of pyridine with $\text{HBr}$ followed by $\text{Br}_2$ forms the crystalline organic salt pyridinium tribromide, $\text{PyH}^+\text{Br}_3^-$ ($\mathbf{X}$), which is a convenient solid source of electrophilic $\text{Br}_2$.
Step 2: Addition of $\text{Br}_2$ (from $\text{PyH}^+\text{Br}_3^-$) to *trans*-stilbene in $\text{AcOH}$ proceeds via a cyclic bromonium ion intermediate with stereospecific *anti*-addition.
Step 3: *Anti*-addition of $\text{Br}_2$ to a *trans*-alkene yields the *meso* dibromide, $(1R,2S)$-1,2-dibromo-1,2-diphenylethane. In the zigzag (anti-periplanar $\text{Ph}$ groups) drawing, both $\text{Br}$ atoms point on the same face (both wedged), corresponding to option (B).

questions.questionTextEn:
The major product of the reaction is:
*cis*-bicyclo[6.2.0]deca-2,9-diene (cyclobutene ring fused *cis* to a cyclooctene ring, both bridgehead $\text{H}$ atoms wedged, double bond in the 8-membered ring adjacent to a bridgehead) $\xrightarrow{150\;^\circ\text{C}}$
optionsEn: *cis*-1,4,4a,5,8,8a-hexahydronaphthalene (both bridgehead $\text{H}$ wedged, two isolated double bonds at $\text{C2}=\text{C3}$ and $\text{C6}=\text{C7}$)
*trans*-1,4,4a,5,8,8a-hexahydronaphthalene (one bridgehead $\text{H}$ wedged, one dashed; two isolated double bonds at $\text{C2}=\text{C3}$ and $\text{C6}=\text{C7}$)
*cis*-4a,5,6,7,8,8a-hexahydronaphthalene (both bridgehead $\text{H}$ wedged; conjugated 1,3-diene in one ring)
*trans*-4a,5,6,7,8,8a-hexahydronaphthalene (one bridgehead $\text{H}$ wedged, one dashed; conjugated 1,3-diene in one ring)
questions.explanationEn:
Step 1: Under thermal conditions ($150\;^\circ\text{C}$), the cyclobutene ring of *cis*-bicyclo[6.2.0]deca-2,9-diene undergoes a Woodward–Hoffmann allowed $4\pi$ **conrotatory** electrocyclic ring opening. Because the ring junction is *cis*, conrotatory opening produces one $(E)$ and one $(Z)$ double bond, yielding $(1E,3Z,5Z)$-cyclodeca-1,3,5-triene.
Step 2: This conjugated 1,3,5-triene immediately undergoes a thermal $6\pi$ **disrotatory** electrocyclic ring closure. For an $(E,Z,Z)$-triene, disrotatory closure places the two terminal hydrogens *trans* to one another, forming *trans*-4a,5,6,7,8,8a-hexahydronaphthalene (a *trans*-fused bicyclo[4.4.0]decadiene containing a conjugated 1,3-diene in one ring).
Hence, option (D) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn:
The major product of the reaction is:
2-methyl-3-(phenylthio)hept-1-ene ($\text{H}_2\text{C}=\text{C(Me)–CH(SPh)–}^n\text{Bu}$) $\xrightarrow{\text{N}_2\text{C(CO}_2\text{Me)}_2,\; \text{CuSO}_4}$
questions.explanationEn:
Step 1: $\text{CuSO}_4$ decomposes dimethyl diazomalonate ($\text{N}_2\text{C(CO}_2\text{Me)}_2$) into an electrophilic copper carbenoid, which is selectively attacked by the nucleophilic sulfur lone pair of the allylic phenyl sulfide to generate a sulfonium ylide.
Step 2: The allylic sulfonium ylide undergoes a facile concerted **[2,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement** (Doyle–Kirmse reaction): the carbanionic malonate carbon bonds to the terminal $=\text{CH}_2$ carbon while the $\text{C–S}$ bond cleaves and the double bond shifts to $\text{C2}=\text{C3}$.
Step 3: This yields $(\text{MeO}_2\text{C})_2\text{C(SPh)–CH}_2\text{–C(Me)}=\text{CH–}^n\text{Bu}$, which is option (B).

questions.questionTextEn:
Adsorption of a gas on a solid surface follows the Langmuir isotherm. If $k_a / k_d = 1.0\text{ bar}^{-1}$, the fraction of adsorption sites occupied by the gas at equilibrium under $2.0\text{ bar}$ pressure of the gas at $25\;^\circ\text{C}$ is
($k_a$ and $k_d$ are the rate constants for adsorption and desorption processes, respectively, at $25\;^\circ\text{C}$)
questions.explanationEn:
According to the Langmuir adsorption isotherm, the fraction of occupied sites ($\theta$) is:
$\theta = \frac{KP}{1 + KP}$, where $K = \frac{k_a}{k_d} = 1.0\text{ bar}^{-1}$ and $P = 2.0\text{ bar}$.
Substituting the values:
$\theta = \frac{1.0 \times 2.0}{1 + (1.0 \times 2.0)} = \frac{2}{3}$.
Hence, option (D) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn:
The vapor pressure of a dilute solution of a non-volatile solute and the vapor pressure of the pure solvent at the same temperature are $P$ and $P^*$, respectively.
$\frac{P^* - P}{P^*}$ is equal to
(Assume that the vapor phase behaves as an ideal gas)
questions.explanationEn:
By Raoult's law for a dilute ideal solution containing a non-volatile solute, the vapor pressure of the solution is $P = x_{\text{solvent}} P^*$, where $x_{\text{solvent}} = 1 - x_{\text{solute}}$.
Rearranging gives the relative lowering of vapor pressure:
$\frac{P^* - P}{P^*} = 1 - x_{\text{solvent}} = x_{\text{solute}}$ (mole fraction of the solute).
Hence, option (D) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn:
The volume of water (in $\text{mL}$) required to be added to a $100\text{ mL}$ solution (aq. $0.1\text{ M}$) of a weak acid ($\text{HA}$) at $25\;^\circ\text{C}$ to double its degree of dissociation is
[Given: $K_a$ of $\text{HA}$ at $25\;^\circ\text{C} = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}$]
questions.explanationEn:
Step 1: Since $K_a = 1.8 \times 10^{-5} \ll C_1 = 0.1\text{ M}$, Ostwald's dilution law gives $\alpha \approx \sqrt{\frac{K_a}{C}}$ (specifically $\alpha_1 \approx \sqrt{1.8 \times 10^{-4}} = 0.0134 \ll 1$).
Step 2: To double the degree of dissociation ($\alpha_2 = 2\alpha_1$), the concentration must decrease by a factor of $4$: $C_2 = \frac{C_1}{4}$, which means the final volume must be $V_2 = 4 V_1 = 4 \times 100\text{ mL} = 400\text{ mL}$.
Step 3: The volume of water to be added is $V_{\text{water}} = V_2 - V_1 = 400 - 100 = 300\text{ mL}$.
Hence, option (C) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn:
The following diagram is obtained in a pH-metric titration of a weak dibasic acid ($\text{H}_2\text{A}$) with a strong base. The point that best represents $[\text{HA}^-] = [\text{A}^{2-}]$ is
[Diagram: pH vs. Volume of base added showing two buffer regions and two steep equivalence jumps: $\mathbf{p}$ is at the midpoint of the first buffer region, $\mathbf{q}$ is at the first equivalence point, $\mathbf{r}$ is at the midpoint of the second buffer region, and $\mathbf{s}$ is at the second equivalence point.]
questions.explanationEn:
In the titration of a weak dibasic acid $\text{H}_2\text{A}$ with a strong base:
- Point $\mathbf{p}$ is the first half-equivalence point (first buffer midpoint), where $[\text{H}_2\text{A}] = [\text{HA}^-]$ and $\text{pH} = \text{p}K_{a1}$.
- Point $\mathbf{q}$ is the first equivalence point, where $\text{HA}^-$ predominates.
- Point $\mathbf{r}$ is the second half-equivalence point (second buffer midpoint), where $[\text{HA}^-] = [\text{A}^{2-}]$ and $\text{pH} = \text{p}K_{a2}$.
- Point $\mathbf{s}$ is the second equivalence point, where $\text{A}^{2-}$ predominates.
Hence, option (C) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn:
Equal number of gas molecules $\mathbf{A}$ (mass $m$ and radius $r$) and $\mathbf{B}$ (mass $2m$ and radius $2r$) are placed in two separate containers of equal volume. At a given temperature, the ratio of the collision frequency of $\mathbf{B}$ to that of $\mathbf{A}$ is
(Assume the gas molecules as hard spheres)
questions.explanationEn:
The collision frequency of a single-component hard-sphere gas is $Z \propto \sigma \bar{v} \left(\frac{N}{V}\right)$, where the collision cross-section $\sigma = \pi d^2 = 4\pi r^2 \propto r^2$ and the mean speed $\bar{v} = \sqrt{\frac{8k_B T}{\pi m}} \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}$.
At the same $N/V$ and $T$, $Z \propto \frac{r^2}{\sqrt{m}}$. Therefore:
$\frac{Z_{\mathbf{B}}}{Z_{\mathbf{A}}} = \left(\frac{r_{\mathbf{B}}}{r_{\mathbf{A}}}\right)^2 \sqrt{\frac{m_{\mathbf{A}}}{m_{\mathbf{B}}}} = \left(\frac{2r}{r}\right)^2 \sqrt{\frac{m}{2m}} = \frac{4}{\sqrt{2}} = 2\sqrt{2}$.
Thus, the ratio is $2\sqrt{2} : 1$, which is option (B).

questions.questionTextEn:
For the given elementary reactions, the steady-state concentration of $\mathbf{X}$ is:
$2\mathbf{P} \xrightarrow{k_1} \mathbf{X}$; $\mathbf{X} \xrightleftharpoons[k_3]{k_2} \mathbf{Q} + \mathbf{R}$; $\mathbf{X} \xrightarrow{k_4} \mathbf{S}$.
questions.explanationEn:
For the given elementary steps, the net rate of change of intermediate $\mathbf{X}$ is:
$\frac{d[\mathbf{X}]}{dt} = k_1[\mathbf{P}]^2 + k_3[\mathbf{Q}][\mathbf{R}] - k_2[\mathbf{X}] - k_4[\mathbf{X}]$.
Applying the steady-state approximation ($\frac{d[\mathbf{X}]}{dt} = 0$):
$(k_2 + k_4)[\mathbf{X}] = k_1[\mathbf{P}]^2 + k_3[\mathbf{Q}][\mathbf{R}] \implies [\mathbf{X}] = \frac{k_1[\mathbf{P}]^2 + k_3[\mathbf{Q}][\mathbf{R}]}{k_2 + k_4}$.
Hence, option (A) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: The separation (in $\text{nm}$) of $\{134\}$ planes of an orthorhombic unit cell (with cell parameters $a = 0.5\text{ nm}$, $b = 0.6\text{ nm}$, and $c = 0.8\text{ nm}$) is
questions.explanationEn:
For an orthorhombic unit cell, the interplanar spacing $d_{hkl}$ is given by:
$\frac{1}{d_{hkl}^2} = \frac{h^2}{a^2} + \frac{k^2}{b^2} + \frac{l^2}{c^2}$.
Substituting $h = 1, k = 3, l = 4$ and $a = 0.5\text{ nm}, b = 0.6\text{ nm}, c = 0.8\text{ nm}$:
$\frac{1}{d_{134}^2} = \left(\frac{1}{0.5}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{3}{0.6}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{4}{0.8}\right)^2 = 2^2 + 5^2 + 5^2 = 4 + 25 + 25 = 54\text{ nm}^{-2}$.
Therefore, $d_{134} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{54}} \approx 0.136\text{ nm}$.
Hence, option (B) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: The transition metal ($\mathbf{M}$) complex that can have all isomers (geometric, linkage, and ionization) is
questions.explanationEn:
For $[\mathbf{M}(\text{NH}_3)_4\text{Br}_2]\text{SCN}$:
- **Geometric isomerism**: Octahedral $\text{MA}_4\text{B}_2$ exhibits *cis* and *trans* isomers.
- **Ionization isomerism**: Exchanging coordinated $\text{Br}^-$ with counter-ion $\text{SCN}^-$ gives $[\mathbf{M}(\text{NH}_3)_4\text{Br}(\text{SCN})]\text{Br}$.
- **Linkage isomerism**: Once $\text{SCN}^-$ enters the coordination sphere, it is an ambidentate ligand capable of coordinating through either $\text{S}$ ($-\text{SCN}$) or $\text{N}$ ($-\text{NCS}$).
Note that in option (D), exchanging $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ with $\text{SCN}^-$ is *hydrate* (solvate) isomerism rather than pure ionization isomerism, while (B) and (C) lack an ambidentate ligand.
Hence, option (A) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: The geometry of $[\text{VO(acac)}_2]$ is
questions.explanationEn:
Vanadyl acetylacetonate, $[\text{VO(acac)}_2]$, is a 5-coordinate $\text{V(IV)}$ ($d^1$) complex.
The two bidentate acetylacetonate ($\text{acac}^-$) ligands occupy the four equatorial (basal) positions, while the strongly $\pi$-bonded oxo ligand ($\text{V}=\text{O}$) occupies the axial (apical) position, resulting in a **square pyramidal** geometry ($C_{2v}$ symmetry).
Hence, option (A) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn:
The products $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ in the following reaction sequence, respectively, are:
$\text{BCl}_3 \xrightarrow{\text{NH}_4\text{Cl in } \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl},\; 150\;^\circ\text{C}} \mathbf{X} \xrightarrow{\text{NaBH}_4} \mathbf{Y}$
questions.explanationEn:
Step 1: Refluxing $\text{BCl}_3$ with $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ in chlorobenzene at $150\;^\circ\text{C}$ yields $B$-trichloroborazine ($\mathbf{X}$):
$3\text{BCl}_3 + 3\text{NH}_4\text{Cl} \rightarrow \text{B}_3\text{N}_3\text{H}_3\text{Cl}_3 + 9\text{HCl}$.
Step 2: Reduction of $B$-trichloroborazine with $\text{NaBH}_4$ replaces the three $\text{B–Cl}$ bonds with $\text{B–H}$ bonds to yield borazine, $\text{B}_3\text{N}_3\text{H}_6$ ($\mathbf{Y}$, also known as inorganic benzene).
Hence, option (B) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: The correct order of the energy of the $d$ orbitals of a square planar complex is
questions.explanationEn:
In a square planar complex ($D_{4h}$ symmetry) with ligands along the $\pm x$ and $\pm y$ axes (derived by removing the axial ligands along $\pm z$ from an octahedron):
- $d_{x^2-y^2}$ points directly at the four ligands and has the highest energy.
- $d_{xy}$ lies in the $xy$ plane between the ligands and is the next highest.
- Removing the axial ligands strongly stabilizes $d_{z^2}$ (below $d_{xy}$) and stabilizes the degenerate $d_{xz}, d_{yz}$ pair even further.
Thus, the standard crystal field splitting order is $d_{xz} = d_{yz} < d_{z^2} < d_{xy} < d_{x^2-y^2}$.
Hence, option (B) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn:
$\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ in the following reactions, respectively, are:
$\text{EtOH} + 2\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \mathbf{X} + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+ + \text{HSO}_4^-$
$\text{HNO}_3 + 2\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \mathbf{Y} + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+ + 2\text{HSO}_4^-$
questions.explanationEn:
Step 1: In concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, ethanol undergoes sulfonation/esterification to form ethyl hydrogen sulfate ($\mathbf{X} = \text{EtOSO}_3\text{H}$), along with $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ and $\text{HSO}_4^-$ (atom and charge balance: $\text{C}_2\text{H}_6\text{O} + 2\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OSO}_3\text{H} + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+ + \text{HSO}_4^-$).
Step 2: Concentrated $\text{HNO}_3$ acts as a base in $100\%$ $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, dehydrating to generate the nitronium ion ($\mathbf{Y} = \text{NO}_2^+$): $\text{HNO}_3 + 2\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{NO}_2^+ + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+ + 2\text{HSO}_4^-$.
Hence, option (C) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: The correct order of energy levels of the molecular orbitals of $\text{N}_2$ is
questions.explanationEn:
In homonuclear diatomic molecules of the second period up to $\text{N}_2$ ($\text{Li}_2$ through $\text{N}_2$), the energy gap between the $2s$ and $2p$ atomic orbitals is small, leading to significant $s$–$p$ mixing between $2\sigma_g$ and $3\sigma_g$.
This $s$–$p$ mixing pushes the $3\sigma_g$ ($\sigma_{2p_z}$) orbital above the degenerate $1\pi_u$ ($\pi_{2p_x}, \pi_{2p_y}$) bonding orbitals.
Therefore, the molecular orbital energy order for $\text{N}_2$ is:
$1\sigma_g < 1\sigma_u < 2\sigma_g < 2\sigma_u < 1\pi_u < 3\sigma_g < 1\pi_g < 3\sigma_u$.
Hence, option (A) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn:
Free heme in aqueous solution when exposed to dioxygen is finally converted to
(circle around iron in the given choices represents the protoporphyrin IX)
questions.explanationEn:
Without the steric protection of the globin protein pocket, free $\text{Fe}^{\text{II}}$ heme in aqueous solution reacts irreversibly with $\text{O}_2$:
1. Reversible $\text{O}_2$ binding forms $(\text{P})\text{Fe}^{\text{II}}\text{–O}_2$.
2. A second free heme reacts to form a $\mu$-peroxo dimer $(\text{P})\text{Fe}^{\text{III}}\text{–O–O–}\text{Fe}^{\text{III}}(\text{P})$.
3. Homolytic cleavage of the $\text{O–O}$ bond produces ferryl $(\text{P})\text{Fe}^{\text{IV}}=\text{O}$, which reacts with another $\text{Fe}^{\text{II}}$ heme to yield the thermodynamically stable $\mu$-oxo $\text{Fe}^{\text{III}}$ dimer (hematin), $(\text{P})\text{Fe}^{\text{III}}\text{–O–}\text{Fe}^{\text{III}}(\text{P})$.
Hence, option (D) is correct.

optionsEn: Both $\mathbf{Q}$ and $\mathbf{R}$ give positive Fehling's test
$\mathbf{Q}$ gives positive iodoform test and its $^1\text{H}$ NMR spectrum shows singlets at $1.0\text{ ppm}$ ($3\text{H}$) and at $1.3\text{ ppm}$ ($3\text{H}$)
$\mathbf{R}$ gives positive iodoform test and its $^1\text{H}$ NMR spectrum shows singlets at $1.0\text{ ppm}$ ($3\text{H}$) and at $2.2\text{ ppm}$ ($3\text{H}$)
A bright yellow precipitate is formed when $\mathbf{Q}$ and $\mathbf{R}$ treated separately with 2,4-dinitrophenyl hydrazine
questions.explanationEn:
Step 1: Under acidic pinacol–pinacolone rearrangement conditions ($\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$):
- *trans*-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane-1,2-diol undergoes a 1,2-methyl shift (anti-periplanar to the leaving axial $\text{H}_2\text{O}^+$) to give **2,2-dimethylcyclohexan-1-one** ($\mathbf{Q}$).
- *cis*-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane-1,2-diol has a ring $\text{C–C}$ bond anti-periplanar to the axial leaving group, undergoing ring contraction to give **1-acetyl-1-methylcyclopentane** ($\mathbf{R}$).
Step 2: Evaluating each statement:
- (A) False: Both $\mathbf{Q}$ and $\mathbf{R}$ are ketones, so neither gives a positive Fehling's test.
- (B) False: $\mathbf{Q}$ (2,2-dimethylcyclohexanone) is not a methyl ketone, so it gives a negative iodoform test, and its two equivalent methyl groups appear as a single $6\text{H}$ singlet.
- (C) True: $\mathbf{R}$ (1-acetyl-1-methylcyclopentane) contains a $-\text{COCH}_3$ group, so it gives a positive iodoform test and shows two $3\text{H}$ singlets in $^1\text{H}$ NMR: the quaternary $-\text{CH}_3$ at $\approx 1.0\text{ ppm}$ and the acetyl $-\text{COCH}_3$ at $\approx 2.2\text{ ppm}$.
- (D) True: Both $\mathbf{Q}$ and $\mathbf{R}$ are ketones and react with 2,4-DNP to give a bright yellow/orange-yellow hydrazone precipitate.
Therefore, options (C) and (D) are correct.

questions.questionTextEn: The correct statement(s) is/are
optionsEn: The $\text{p}K_{a1}$ of *cis*-cyclohexane-1,3-diol is greater than that of the *trans* isomer.
The *trans*-4-(*tert*-butyl)cyclohexanamine is more basic than its *cis* isomer.
2,6-Dihydroxybenzoic acid is more acidic than salicylic acid.
questions.explanationEn:
- (A) False: In *cis*-cyclohexane-1,3-diol, both $\text{OH}$ groups can adopt a diaxial conformation allowing intramolecular hydrogen bonding that stabilizes the mono-alkoxide conjugate base. This makes the *cis* isomer *more* acidic (lower $\text{p}K_{a1}$) than the *trans* isomer.
- (B) True: In *trans*-4-(*tert*-butyl)cyclohexanamine, the $-\text{NH}_2$ group is equatorial, so its protonated conjugate acid ($-\text{NH}_3^+$) is less sterically hindered and better solvated than the axial $-\text{NH}_3^+$ of the *cis* isomer; hence the *trans* isomer is more basic.
- (C) True: 2,6-Dihydroxybenzoic acid ($\text{p}K_a \approx 1.30$) is significantly more acidic than salicylic acid ($\text{p}K_a \approx 2.97$) because both *ortho*-$\text{OH}$ groups form strong intramolecular hydrogen bonds with the carboxylate anion (and sterically inhibit carboxyl resonance).
- (D) Ambiguous in literature: Picric acid (2,4,6-trinitrophenol) has $\text{p}K_a \approx 0.38$, while 2,4,6-trinitrobenzoic acid has $\text{p}K_a \approx 0.65$ (making picric acid slightly stronger in water), though some textbooks cite carboxylic acids as stronger. Accordingly, the official IIT Guwahati Final Answer Key accepts **both (B, C) and (B, C, D)**.

questions.questionTextEn: The reaction(s) that yield(s) $\text{Ph–CH}_2\text{–CH}_2\text{–CO}_2\text{Me}$ as the major product is/are
questions.explanationEn:
We need reactions producing methyl 3-phenylpropanoate ($\text{Ph–CH}_2\text{–CH}_2\text{–CO}_2\text{Me}$):
- (A) $\text{Ph–CH}_2\text{Br}$ undergoes $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ with $\text{NaCN}$ to give $\text{Ph–CH}_2\text{CN}$, which upon hydrolysis and esterification gives $\text{Ph–CH}_2\text{–CO}_2\text{Me}$ (one carbon shorter). False.
- (B) 1-Chloro-1-phenylpropan-2-one with $\text{NaOMe}$ undergoes the **Favorskii rearrangement** via a 2-phenylcyclopropanone intermediate. Nucleophilic ring opening by $\text{MeO}^-$ selectively cleaves the bond forming the more stable benzylic carbanion, yielding $\text{Ph–CH}_2\text{–CH}_2\text{–CO}_2\text{Me}$. True.
- (C) 1-Chloro-3-phenylpropan-2-one with $\text{NaOMe}$ forms the exact same 2-phenylcyclopropanone intermediate in the Favorskii rearrangement, also giving $\text{Ph–CH}_2\text{–CH}_2\text{–CO}_2\text{Me}$. True.
- (D) Phenylacetic acid undergoes **Arndt–Eistert homologation** via acid chloride $\rightarrow$ $\alpha$-diazoketone $\rightarrow$ Wolff rearrangement in $\text{MeOH}$ to yield the one-carbon homologated methyl ester $\text{Ph–CH}_2\text{–CH}_2\text{–CO}_2\text{Me}$. True.
Therefore, options (B), (C), and (D) are correct.

questions.questionTextEn:
The correct option(s) of the reagents required for the following reaction is/are:
Cyclopent-2-en-1-one $\xrightarrow{\text{reagents}}$ 3-ethylcyclopentan-1-one
questions.explanationEn:
The transformation is a 1,4-conjugate addition of an ethyl group to an $\alpha,\beta$-unsaturated ketone:
- (A) True: $\text{Et}_3\text{B}$ with catalytic $\text{O}_2$ initiates a free-radical chain 1,4-conjugate addition of ethyl radicals to cyclopent-2-en-1-one, giving a boron enolate that hydrolyzes with $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to 3-ethylcyclopentan-1-one.
- (B) True: Gilman cuprate ($\text{Et}_2\text{CuLi}$) in the presence of $\text{Me}_3\text{SiCl}$ performs clean 1,4-conjugate addition to give the silyl enol ether, which hydrolyzes with $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ to 3-ethylcyclopentan-1-one.
- (C) False: Hard Grignard reagent $\text{EtMgBr}$ without a copper catalyst predominantly gives 1,2-addition (1-ethylcyclopent-2-en-1-ol).
- (D) False: $^n\text{BuLi}$ is a hard nucleophile that attacks the carbonyl carbon (1,2-addition) rather than giving $\beta$-ethylation.
Therefore, options (A) and (B) are correct.

questions.questionTextEn: The reaction(s) that yield(s) 1-naphthol as the major product is/are
questions.explanationEn:
- (A) True: 1-Bromo-2-fluorobenzene with $\text{Li–Hg}$ generates benzyne, which undergoes Diels–Alder cycloaddition with furan to form 1,4-epoxy-1,4-dihydronaphthalene; acid-catalyzed ring opening and aromatization yield **1-naphthol**.
- (B) False: Clemmensen reduction ($\text{Zn–Hg/HCl}$) reduces 1-tetralone to tetralin, and subsequent dehydrogenation with $\text{Pd–C}$/heat yields **naphthalene** (not 1-naphthol).
- (C) True: Heating 4-phenylbut-3-enoic acid with $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ triggers intramolecular Friedel–Crafts acylation to form a naphthalenone that immediately tautomerizes to **1-naphthol**.
- (D) True: Baeyer–Villiger oxidation of 1-acetylnaphthalene with $m$-CPBA proceeds with preferential migration of the 1-naphthyl group over methyl to give 1-naphthyl acetate, which hydrolyzes to **1-naphthol**.
Therefore, options (A), (C), and (D) are correct.

questions.questionTextEn: The correct relation(s) for an ideal gas in a closed system is/are
questions.explanationEn:
For an ideal gas, enthalpy $H = U + PV = U(T) + nRT$ is a function of temperature $T$ alone.
- (A) True: Since $H$ depends only on $T$, $\left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial V}\right)_T = 0$.
- (B) True: The Joule–Thomson coefficient is $\mu_{\text{JT}} = \left(\frac{\partial T}{\partial P}\right)_H = -\frac{1}{C_P}\left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial P}\right)_T = 0$ for an ideal gas.
- (C) True: Since $H$ depends only on $T$, $\left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial P}\right)_T = 0$.
- (D) False: $\left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial T}\right)_P = C_P \neq 0$ (for an ideal gas, $C_P \ge \frac{5}{2}nR > 0$).
Therefore, options (A), (B), and (C) are correct.

questions.questionTextEn: The molecule(s) that follow(s) $I_a < I_b = I_c$ ($I_a$, $I_b$, and $I_c$ are the principal moments of inertia) is/are
questions.explanationEn:
The condition $I_a < I_b = I_c$ describes both linear molecules ($I_a = 0 < I_b = I_c$) and prolate symmetric tops ($0 < I_a < I_b = I_c$):
- (A) $\text{HCN}$ is linear ($C_{\infty v}$): $I_a = 0 < I_b = I_c$. True.
- (B) $\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}$ ($C_{3v}$) is a prolate symmetric top: $0 < I_a < I_b = I_c$. True.
- (C) $\text{CH}_3\text{C}\equiv\text{CH}$ (propyne, $C_{3v}$) is a prolate symmetric top: $0 < I_a < I_b = I_c$. True.
- (D) $\text{C}_6\text{H}_6$ (benzene, $D_{6h}$) is an oblate symmetric top, where $I_a = I_b < I_c$. False.
Therefore, options (A), (B), and (C) are correct.

questions.questionTextEn: The role(s) of fluorspar in the electrolytic reduction of $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ is/are to
optionsEn: improve the electrical conductivity of the melt
prevent the radiation loss of heat
questions.explanationEn:
In the Hall–Héroult process for electrolytic extraction of aluminium from alumina ($\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$, melting point $\approx 2072\;^\circ\text{C}$), cryolite ($\text{Na}_3\text{AlF}_6$) and fluorspar ($\text{CaF}_2$) are added to:
- (A) True: Lower the melting point of the electrolyte mixture to about $950\text{–}980\;^\circ\text{C}$.
- (B) True: Increase the fluidity and electrical conductivity of the molten bath.
- (C) & (D) False: Powdered coke spread over the molten bath prevents heat loss by radiation and protects the carbon anodes from atmospheric oxidation, not fluorspar.
Therefore, options (A) and (B) are correct.

questions.questionTextEn: The correct statement(s) about the complexes $\mathbf{I}$ ($\text{K}_3[\text{CoF}_6]$) and $\mathbf{II}$ ($\text{K}_3[\text{RhF}_6]$) is/are
optionsEn: The crystal field stabilization energy of complex $\mathbf{II}$ is more than that of complex $\mathbf{I}$.
questions.explanationEn:
Both $\text{Co}^{3+}$ ($3d^6$) and $\text{Rh}^{3+}$ ($4d^6$) are $d^6$ octahedral complexes with weak-field $\text{F}^-$ ligands:
- Complex $\mathbf{I}$ ($[\text{CoF}_6]^{3-}$): $\text{Co}^{3+}$ is a $3d$ ion with weak-field $\text{F}^-$, so it is **high spin** ($t_{2g}^4 e_g^2$, $4$ unpaired electrons $\implies$ **paramagnetic**), with $\text{CFSE} = (-0.4 \times 4 + 0.6 \times 2)\Delta_o = -0.4\Delta_o$.
- Complex $\mathbf{II}$ ($[\text{RhF}_6]^{3-}$): $\text{Rh}^{3+}$ is a $4d$ metal ion, which has a much larger crystal field splitting $\Delta_o$ (typically $\approx 40\text{–}50\%$ larger than $3d$) and lower pairing energy, so it is **low spin** ($t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$, $0$ unpaired electrons $\implies$ **diamagnetic**), with $\text{CFSE} = -2.4\Delta_o + 2P$.
- Therefore, (A) is False, while (B), (C), and (D) are True (both in magnitude of $\Delta_o$ and CFSE).

questions.questionTextEn: The diatomic molecule(s) that has/have bond order of one is/are
questions.explanationEn:
Using Molecular Orbital Theory, $\text{Bond Order} = \frac{N_b - N_a}{2}$:
- (A) $\text{B}_2$ ($10\text{ e}^-$): $(\sigma_{1s})^2(\sigma^*_{1s})^2(\sigma_{2s})^2(\sigma^*_{2s})^2(\pi_{2p_x})^1(\pi_{2p_y})^1 \implies \text{BO} = \frac{6 - 4}{2} = 1$. True.
- (B) $\text{N}_2^{2-}$ ($16\text{ e}^-$): Two electrons occupy $\pi^*_{2p}$ orbitals beyond $\text{N}_2$ ($\text{BO} = 3$) $\implies \text{BO} = 3 - 1 = 2$. False.
- (C) $\text{Li}_2$ ($6\text{ e}^-$): $(\sigma_{1s})^2(\sigma^*_{1s})^2(\sigma_{2s})^2 \implies \text{BO} = \frac{4 - 2}{2} = 1$. True.
- (D) $\text{O}_2^{2-}$ ($18\text{ e}^-$): Two electrons fill $\pi^*_{2p}$ beyond $\text{O}_2$ ($\text{BO} = 2$) $\implies \text{BO} = 2 - 1 = 1$. True.
Therefore, options (A), (C), and (D) are correct.

questions.questionTextEn:
The molecular weight of the major product of the reaction is ______ (in integer).
4-nitroaniline $\xrightarrow{\text{(i) } \text{Br}_2\text{ (excess)},\; \text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H};\; \text{(ii) } \text{Sn/HCl};\; \text{(iii) } \text{NaNO}_2/\text{HCl (excess)},\; 0\;^\circ\text{C};\; \text{(iv) } \text{CuBr (excess)}}$
[Given: atomic weight of $\text{H} = 1$, $\text{C} = 12$, $\text{N} = 14$, and $\text{Br} = 80$]
questions.explanationEn:
Step 1: Excess $\text{Br}_2/\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ brominates the two *ortho* positions activated by $-\text{NH}_2$ on 4-nitroaniline to form 2,6-dibromo-4-nitroaniline.
Step 2: $\text{Sn/HCl}$ reduces the $-\text{NO}_2$ group to $-\text{NH}_2$, giving 2,6-dibromobenzene-1,4-diamine.
Step 3: Excess $\text{NaNO}_2/\text{HCl}$ at $0\;^\circ\text{C}$ diazotizes both $-\text{NH}_2$ groups to form the bis-diazonium salt.
Step 4: Excess $\text{CuBr}$ (Sandmeyer reaction) replaces both diazonium groups with $-\text{Br}$, yielding **1,2,3,5-tetrabromobenzene** ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_2\text{Br}_4$).
Step 5: Molecular weight $= 6(12) + 2(1) + 4(80) = 72 + 2 + 320 = 394$.

questions.questionTextEn:
A $0.06\text{ g/mL}$ solution of $(S)$-1-phenylethanol placed in a $5\text{ cm}$ long polarimeter tube shows an optical rotation of $1.2^\circ$. The specific rotation is ______ $^\circ$.
(round off to the nearest integer)
questions.explanationEn:
Specific rotation is given by $[\alpha] = \frac{\alpha_{\text{obs}}}{l \times c}$, where:
- $\alpha_{\text{obs}} = 1.2^\circ$
- $l = 5\text{ cm} = 0.5\text{ dm}$
- $c = 0.06\text{ g mL}^{-1}$
Substituting the values:
$[\alpha] = \frac{1.2}{0.5 \times 0.06} = \frac{1.2}{0.03} = 40^\circ$.

questions.questionTextEn:
The isoelectric point of glutamic acid is ______.
[Structure given: $\text{HO}_2\text{C–CH}_2\text{–CH}_2\text{–CH(NH}_3^+)\text{–CO}_2\text{H}$, with side-chain $\text{p}K_a = 4.25$, $\alpha$-carboxyl $\text{p}K_a = 2.19$, and $\alpha$-ammonium $\text{p}K_a = 9.67$.]
(round off to two decimal places)
questions.explanationEn:
Glutamic acid is an acidic amino acid; its neutral zwitterionic form lies between the deprotonation of the $\alpha$-carboxyl group ($\text{p}K_{a1} = 2.19$) and the side-chain $\gamma$-carboxyl group ($\text{p}K_{aR} = 4.25$).
Therefore, the isoelectric point ($\text{pI}$) is the average of the two lower $\text{p}K_a$ values:
$\text{pI} = \frac{\text{p}K_{a1} + \text{p}K_{aR}}{2} = \frac{2.19 + 4.25}{2} = \frac{6.44}{2} = 3.22$.

questions.questionTextEn:
Consider the following reaction:
$2\text{C}_6\text{H}_6 + 15\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 12\text{CO}_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O} \qquad \Delta_r H^0_{298} = -3120\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$.
A closed system initially contains $5\text{ moles}$ of benzene and $25\text{ moles}$ of oxygen under standard conditions at $298\text{ K}$. The reaction was stopped when $17.5\text{ moles}$ of oxygen is left. The amount of heat evolved during the reaction is ______ $\text{kJ}$.
(round off to the nearest integer)
questions.explanationEn:
Step 1: Moles of $\text{O}_2$ consumed $= 25 - 17.5 = 7.5\text{ mol}$.
Step 2: From the stoichiometry, $15\text{ mol}$ of $\text{O}_2$ corresponds to $1\text{ mol}$ extent of reaction ($\xi = 1\text{ mol}$), so:
$\xi = \frac{7.5}{15} = 0.5\text{ mol}$ (consuming $1.0\text{ mol}$ of $\text{C}_6\text{H}_6$, well within the $5\text{ mol}$ initially present).
Step 3: Enthalpy change $\Delta H = \xi \cdot \Delta_r H^0_{298} = 0.5 \times (-3120) = -1560\text{ kJ}$.
Thus, the amount of heat evolved is $1560\text{ kJ}$.

questions.questionTextEn:
For the elementary reaction $\mathbf{C} \xleftarrow{k_2} \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow{k_1} \mathbf{B}$, $k_1 = 2k_2$. At time $t = 0$, $[\mathbf{A}] = A_0$ and $[\mathbf{B}] = [\mathbf{C}] = 0$. At a later time $t$, the value of $[\mathbf{B}]/[\mathbf{C}]$ is ______.
(round off to the nearest integer)
questions.explanationEn:
For parallel first-order reactions $\mathbf{A} \xrightarrow{k_1} \mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{A} \xrightarrow{k_2} \mathbf{C}$ with $[\mathbf{B}]_0 = [\mathbf{C}]_0 = 0$:
$[\mathbf{B}] = \frac{k_1}{k_1 + k_2} A_0 \left(1 - e^{-(k_1+k_2)t}\right)$ and $[\mathbf{C}] = \frac{k_2}{k_1 + k_2} A_0 \left(1 - e^{-(k_1+k_2)t}\right)$.
Taking the ratio at any time $t > 0$:
$\frac{[\mathbf{B}]}{[\mathbf{C}]} = \frac{k_1}{k_2} = 2$.

questions.questionTextEn:
The highest possible energy of a photon in the emission spectrum of hydrogen atom is ______ $\text{eV}$.
[Given: Rydberg constant $= 13.61\text{ eV}$]
(round off to two decimal places)
questions.explanationEn:
The highest-energy photon in the hydrogen emission spectrum corresponds to the Lyman series limit, i.e., the transition from $n_2 = \infty$ to $n_1 = 1$:
$\Delta E_{\max} = R_H \left(\frac{1}{1^2} - \frac{1}{\infty^2}\right) = 13.61\text{ eV}$.

questions.questionTextEn:
The standard reduction potential ($E^0$) of $\text{Fe}^{3+} \rightarrow \text{Fe}$ is ______ $\text{V}$.
[Given: $\text{Fe}^{3+} \rightarrow \text{Fe}^{2+} \quad E^0 = 0.77\text{ V}$ and $\text{Fe}^{2+} \rightarrow \text{Fe} \quad E^0 = -0.44\text{ V}$]
(round off to three decimal places)
questions.explanationEn:
Since $\Delta G^0 = -nFE^0$ is an extensive state function, adding the two half-reactions gives:
$\Delta G^0_3 = \Delta G^0_1 + \Delta G^0_2 \implies -3FE^0_3 = -1F(0.77) - 2F(-0.44)$.
Therefore:
$E^0(\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}) = \frac{1(0.77) + 2(-0.44)}{3} = \frac{0.77 - 0.88}{3} = \frac{-0.11}{3} \approx -0.0367\text{ V} \approx -0.037\text{ V}$.

questions.questionTextEn: The number of valence electrons in $\text{Na}_2[\text{Fe(CO)}_4]$ (the Collman's reagent) is ______.
questions.explanationEn:
In Collman's reagent, $\text{Na}_2[\text{Fe(CO)}_4]$, the organometallic anion is $[\text{Fe(CO)}_4]^{2-}$:
- Neutral $\text{Fe}$ (group 8) contributes $8$ valence electrons.
- The $2-$ charge contributes $2$ electrons (so $\text{Fe}^{2-}$ is $d^{10}$).
- Four neutral $\text{CO}$ ligands contribute $4 \times 2 = 8$ electrons.
Total valence electron count $= 8 + 2 + 8 = 18$.

questions.questionTextEn:
In the Born–Haber cycle, the heat of formation of $\text{CuCl}$ is ______ $\text{kJ/mol}$.
[Given: Heat of atomization of $\text{Cu} = +338\text{ kJ/mol}$, Ionization energy of $\text{Cu} = +746\text{ kJ/mol}$, Heat of atomization of $\text{Cl}_2 = +121\text{ kJ/mol}$, Electron affinity of $\text{Cl} = -349\text{ kJ/mol}$, and Lattice energy of $\text{CuCl} = -973\text{ kJ/mol}$]
(round off to the nearest integer)
questions.explanationEn:
For $\text{Cu(s)} + \frac{1}{2}\text{Cl}_2\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{CuCl(s)}$, the Born–Haber cycle gives:
$\Delta H_f^\circ(\text{CuCl}) = \Delta H_{\text{atom}}(\text{Cu}) + \text{IE}(\text{Cu}) + \Delta H_{\text{atom}}(\text{Cl}) + \text{EA}(\text{Cl}) + U_{\text{lattice}}(\text{CuCl})$.
- **Interpretation 1 (standard definition of heat of atomization per mole of $\text{Cl}$ atoms, $\frac{1}{2}\text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow \text{Cl} = +121\text{ kJ/mol}$)**:
$\Delta H_f^\circ = 338 + 746 + 121 - 349 - 973 = -117\text{ kJ/mol}$.
- **Interpretation 2 (if $+121\text{ kJ/mol}$ is taken per mole of $\text{Cl}_2$, using $\frac{1}{2} \times 121 = 60.5\text{ kJ/mol}$)**:
$\Delta H_f^\circ = 338 + 746 + 60.5 - 349 - 973 = -177.5\text{ kJ/mol}$ (rounds to $-178$ or $-177$).
Accordingly, the official IIT Guwahati Final Answer Key accepts **$-117$ or $-178$ to $-177$**.

questions.questionTextEn:
The spin-only magnetic moment of $\text{B}_2$ molecule is ______ $\mu_B$.
(round off to two decimal places)
questions.explanationEn:
The molecular orbital configuration of $\text{B}_2$ ($10\text{ e}^-$) is:
$(1\sigma_g)^2 (1\sigma_u)^2 (2\sigma_g)^2 (2\sigma_u)^2 (1\pi_{u,x})^1 (1\pi_{u,y})^1$.
Because there are $n = 2$ unpaired electrons in the degenerate $1\pi_u$ orbitals, the spin-only magnetic moment is:
$\mu_s = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\,\mu_B = \sqrt{2(2+2)}\,\mu_B = \sqrt{8}\,\mu_B \approx 2.83\,\mu_B$.

questions.questionTextEn:
The sum of the total number of stereoisomers (including enantiomers) present in the following molecules is ______.
[Two molecules shown: (1) butane-2,3-diol ($\text{Me–CH(OH)–CH(OH)–Me}$, both $\text{OH}$ bonds wavy); (2) *trans*-decahydronaphthalen-2-amine (decalin ring with one bridgehead $\text{H}$ wedged and the other bridgehead $\text{H}$ dashed, and a wavy bond to $-\text{NH}_2$ at $\text{C2}$).]
questions.explanationEn:
Step 1: **Butane-2,3-diol** has two identically substituted chiral centers ($\text{C2}$ and $\text{C3}$), giving **$3$ stereoisomers**: one *meso* form $(2R,3S)$ and one enantiomeric pair $(2R,3R)/(2S,3S)$.
Step 2: ***trans*-Decahydronaphthalen-2-amine**:
- If the drawn *trans* ring junction (top bridgehead $\text{H}$ wedged, bottom bridgehead $\text{H}$ dashed) is treated as a **single fixed configuration**, then varying the wavy $\text{C2–NH}_2$ bond gives **$2$ diastereomers** (equatorial vs. axial $\text{NH}_2$), making the sum $3 + 2 = 5$.
- If **both enantiomeric *trans* ring junctions** ($(4\text{a}R,8\text{a}R)$ and $(4\text{a}S,8\text{a}S)$) are included along with $(R)/(S)$ at $\text{C2}$, there are **$4$ stereoisomers** (two enantiomeric pairs), making the sum $3 + 4 = 7$.
Accordingly, the official IIT Guwahati Final Answer Key accepts **both $5$ and $7$**.

questions.questionTextEn:
The number of singlets observed in the $^1\text{H}$ NMR spectrum of $\mathbf{P}$ is ______.
[$\mathbf{P}$: 1-bromo-4-methoxy-2,6-dimethylbenzene (benzene ring with $-\text{Br}$ at $\text{C1}$, $-\text{Me}$ at $\text{C2}$ and $\text{C6}$, and $-\text{OMe}$ at $\text{C4}$).]
questions.explanationEn:
1-Bromo-4-methoxy-2,6-dimethylbenzene ($\mathbf{P}$) possesses a vertical plane of symmetry passing through $\text{C1(Br)}$ and $\text{C4(OMe)}$, giving three chemically non-equivalent sets of protons with no vicinal ($^3J$) coupling partners:
1. Two equivalent $-\text{CH}_3$ groups at $\text{C2}$ and $\text{C6}$ $\rightarrow 1$ singlet ($6\text{H}$).
2. Two equivalent aromatic protons at $\text{C3}$ and $\text{C5}$ $\rightarrow 1$ singlet ($2\text{H}$).
3. One $-\text{OCH}_3$ group at $\text{C4}$ $\rightarrow 1$ singlet ($3\text{H}$).
Hence, the total number of singlets observed is $3$.

questions.questionTextEn:
When a glass capillary tube is dipped in water, a $1.0\text{ cm}$ rise in the water level is observed at $18\;^\circ\text{C}$. The internal radius of the capillary is ______ $\text{cm}$.
[Given: Surface tension of water at $18\;^\circ\text{C} = 73.2\text{ dyne cm}^{-1}$; difference in the densities of water and air at $18\;^\circ\text{C} = 0.996\text{ g cm}^{-3}$; gravitational acceleration constant, $g = 980\text{ cm s}^{-2}$.
Assume that water completely wets the glass capillary and the interface between the water and the air phase inside the capillary is a hemisphere.]
(round off to two decimal places)
questions.explanationEn:
For complete wetting (contact angle $\theta = 0^\circ$, $\cos\theta = 1$), the capillary rise formula is:
$h = \frac{2\gamma}{r\Delta\rho g} \implies r = \frac{2\gamma}{h\Delta\rho g}$.
Substituting $\gamma = 73.2\text{ dyne cm}^{-1}$, $h = 1.0\text{ cm}$, $\Delta\rho = 0.996\text{ g cm}^{-3}$, and $g = 980\text{ cm s}^{-2}$:
$r = \frac{2 \times 73.2}{1.0 \times 0.996 \times 980} = \frac{146.4}{976.08} \approx 0.14999\text{ cm} \approx 0.15\text{ cm}$.

questions.questionTextEn:
The volume of $2.0\text{ mol}$ of an ideal gas is reduced to half isothermally at $300\text{ K}$ in a closed system. The value of $\Delta G$ is ______ $\text{kJ}$.
[Given: $R = 8.314\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$]
(round off to two decimal places)
questions.explanationEn:
For an isothermal process of an ideal gas, the Gibbs free energy change is:
$\Delta G = nRT\ln\left(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\right) = nRT\ln\left(\frac{V_1}{V_2}\right)$.
With $n = 2.0\text{ mol}$, $T = 300\text{ K}$, $R = 8.314\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$, and $V_1/V_2 = 2$:
$\Delta G = 2.0 \times 8.314 \times 300 \times \ln(2) = 4988.4 \times 0.69315 \approx 3457.7\text{ J} = 3.46\text{ kJ}$.

questions.questionTextEn:
The harmonic vibrational frequency of a diatomic molecule is $2000\text{ cm}^{-1}$. Its zero-point energy is ______ $\text{eV}$.
[Given: Planck's constant $= 6.62 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J s}$; $1\text{ eV} = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}$]
(round off to two decimal places)
questions.explanationEn:
The zero-point energy of a harmonic oscillator is $E_0 = \frac{1}{2}h\nu = \frac{1}{2}hc\tilde{\nu}$.
Using $h = 6.62 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J s}$, $c = 3.0 \times 10^{10}\text{ cm s}^{-1}$, and $\tilde{\nu} = 2000\text{ cm}^{-1}$:
$E_0 = 0.5 \times 6.62 \times 10^{-34} \times 3.0 \times 10^{10} \times 2000 = 1.986 \times 10^{-20}\text{ J}$.
Converting to electron-volts:
$E_0 = \frac{1.986 \times 10^{-20}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 0.1241\text{ eV} \approx 0.12\text{ eV}$.

questions.questionTextEn:
An elementary reaction $2\mathbf{A} \rightarrow \mathbf{P}$ follows a second order rate law with rate constant $2.5 \times 10^{-3}\text{ dm}^3\text{ mol}^{-1}\text{ s}^{-1}$. The time required for the concentration of $\mathbf{A}$ to change from $0.4\text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ to $0.2\text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ is ______ $\text{s}$.
(round off to the nearest integer)
questions.explanationEn:
For the elementary reaction $2\mathbf{A} \rightarrow \mathbf{P}$, the rate of reaction is:
$r = -\frac{1}{2}\frac{d[\mathbf{A}]}{dt} = k[\mathbf{A}]^2 \implies -\frac{d[\mathbf{A}]}{dt} = 2k[\mathbf{A}]^2$.
Integrating from $[\mathbf{A}]_0 = 0.4\text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ to $[\mathbf{A}]_t = 0.2\text{ mol dm}^{-3}$:
$\frac{1}{[\mathbf{A}]_t} - \frac{1}{[\mathbf{A}]_0} = 2kt \implies \frac{1}{0.2} - \frac{1}{0.4} = 2(2.5 \times 10^{-3})t$.
$5 - 2.5 = 5.0 \times 10^{-3}\,t \implies t = \frac{2.5}{5.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 500\text{ s}$.

questions.questionTextEn:
The following diagram shows the kinetic energy of the ejected photoelectrons against the energy of incident radiation for two metal surfaces $\mathbf{M}_1$ and $\mathbf{M}_2$. If the energy of the incident radiation on $\mathbf{M}_1$ is equal to the work function of $\mathbf{M}_2$, the de Broglie wavelength of the ejected photoelectron is ______ $\text{nm}$.
[Diagram: Straight-line plots of Kinetic energy of photoelectrons vs. Energy of incident radiation ($\text{eV}$) with $x$-intercepts (work functions) at $2.3\text{ eV}$ for $\mathbf{M}_1$ and $2.9\text{ eV}$ for $\mathbf{M}_2$.]
[Given: Mass of electron $= 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}$; Planck's constant $= 6.62 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J s}$; $1\text{ eV} = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}$.]
(round off to two decimal places)
questions.explanationEn:
Step 1: From the $x$-intercepts of the photoelectric plots, the work functions are $\phi_1 = 2.3\text{ eV}$ (for $\mathbf{M}_1$) and $\phi_2 = 2.9\text{ eV}$ (for $\mathbf{M}_2$).
Step 2: When radiation of energy $E = \phi_2 = 2.9\text{ eV}$ strikes $\mathbf{M}_1$, the kinetic energy of the ejected photoelectron is:
$\text{KE} = E - \phi_1 = 2.9 - 2.3 = 0.6\text{ eV} = 0.6 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J} = 9.6 \times 10^{-20}\text{ J}$.
Step 3: The de Broglie wavelength is:
$\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2m_e \cdot \text{KE}}} = \frac{6.62 \times 10^{-34}}{\sqrt{2 \times 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \times 9.6 \times 10^{-20}}} = \frac{6.62 \times 10^{-34}}{4.1823 \times 10^{-25}} = 1.5829 \times 10^{-9}\text{ m} \approx 1.58\text{ nm}$.

questions.questionTextEn:
The spin-only magnetic moment of $[\text{Fe(acac)}_3]$ is ______ $\mu_B$.
(round off to two decimal places)
questions.explanationEn:
In $[\text{Fe(acac)}_3]$, iron is in the $+3$ oxidation state ($\text{Fe}^{3+}$, $3d^5$).
Acetylacetonate ($\text{acac}^-$) is a weak-field oxygen-donor ligand, so $[\text{Fe(acac)}_3]$ is an octahedral high-spin $d^5$ complex ($t_{2g}^3 e_g^2$) with $n = 5$ unpaired electrons.
The spin-only magnetic moment is:
$\mu_s = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\,\mu_B = \sqrt{5(5+2)}\,\mu_B = \sqrt{35}\,\mu_B \approx 5.92\,\mu_B$.

questions.questionTextEn:
The amount of ethane produced in the following reaction is ______ $\text{kg}$.
$\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\,(2\text{ kg}) + \text{H}_2\,(2\text{ kg}) \xrightarrow{\text{Wilkinson's Catalyst}} \text{C}_2\text{H}_6$ ($90\%$ catalytic conversion)
(round off to two decimal places)
questions.explanationEn:
Step 1: Determine the limiting reagent (molar masses: $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4 = 28\text{ g mol}^{-1}$, $\text{H}_2 = 2\text{ g mol}^{-1}$, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_6 = 30\text{ g mol}^{-1}$):
- Moles of $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4 = \frac{2000\text{ g}}{28\text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 71.43\text{ mol}$.
- Moles of $\text{H}_2 = \frac{2000\text{ g}}{2\text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 1000\text{ mol}$.
Thus, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$ is the limiting reagent.
Step 2: At $90\%$ conversion, the mass of ethane produced is:
$m(\text{C}_2\text{H}_6) = \frac{2\text{ kg}}{28} \times 30 \times 0.90 = 1.9286\text{ kg} \approx 1.93\text{ kg}$.

questions.questionTextEn:
In a gravimetric estimation of $\text{Al}$, a sample of $0.1000\text{ g}$ $\text{AlCl}_3$ is precipitated with 8-hydroxyquinoline. The weight of the precipitate is ______ $\text{g}$.
[Given: atomic weight of $\text{Al}$ is $26.98$; molecular weight of $\text{AlCl}_3$ is $133.34$; and molecular weight of 8-hydroxyquinoline is $145.16$]
(round off to $4$ decimal places)
questions.explanationEn:
Step 1: $\text{Al}^{3+}$ precipitates quantitatively with 8-hydroxyquinoline ($\text{C}_9\text{H}_7\text{NO}$, oxine, $\text{HOx}$) as tris(8-hydroxyquinolinato)aluminium(III), $\text{Al(C}_9\text{H}_6\text{NO)}_3$ ($\text{Al(Ox)}_3$).
Step 2: Molar mass of the precipitate $\text{Al(Ox)}_3$:
$M(\text{Al(Ox)}_3) = 26.98 + 3 \times (145.16 - 1.008) = 26.98 + 432.456 = 459.436\text{ g mol}^{-1}$ (or $459.46\text{ g mol}^{-1}$ using $\text{H} = 1.00$).
Step 3: Moles of $\text{Al} = \frac{0.1000}{133.34} = 7.4996 \times 10^{-4}\text{ mol}$.
Weight of precipitate $= 7.4996 \times 10^{-4} \times 459.436 = 0.3446\text{ g}$.
